messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Bayes Factors via product spaces?
parts:
I was not able to definitively answer Martin Smira's question
about whether it would be possible to implement the product-space
approach to Bayes factor computations with HMC.

This was developed by Carlin and Chib:

B.P. Carlin, S. Chib
Bayesian model choice via Markov chain Monte Carlo methods
Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 57 (1995), pp. 473–484

There's also an overview in a (paywalled) psych journal that kicked
off the discussion (Lee and Wagenmakers are two of the co-authors):

http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022249611000423

And there's a discussion by Charles Geyer in the umbrella sampling chapter of
the MCMC Handbook (not one of the free chapters, I'm afraid).

The most explicit reference I saw for how a model like this can be
coded is in a BUGS vol2 example:

http://www.medicine.mcgill.ca/epidemiology/joseph/courses/EPIB-682/pines.pdf

We do not have that example working in Stan, nor could I get a version
working. From what I can tell, the product-space approach simulates a reversible
jump MCMC method with Gibbs sampling and pseudo-priors, with some fiddly
pre-tuning required to adjust the pseudo-priors. But I'm afraid I don't even
understand why it'd work in BUGS because the posterior just looks wrong (so there's
probably something I'm not understanding --- like maybe they only take the parameter
samples from one of the branches [which clearly won't work in Stan]).

I had problems trying to conceptualize what the model would even look
like in Stan and was wondering if anyone had any suggestions or an explanation
of why it wouldn't be possible.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayes Factors via product spaces?
parts:
You're always in one model or the other in Stan, too.
It's just that we marginalize out the mixture indicator
parameter. That should just make computation more efficient.

The key to implementing anything in Stan is to understand
what density you want to fit. If you can write the model
down in JAGS, that will determine the density you're fitting.
Then we should be able to code it in Stan directly.

- Bob


> On Mar 22, 2016, at 11:52 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Is there any update on this thus far? I happened to stumble on this post from googling about a stan implementation of the product space method.
>
> Intuitively it seems like one could implement a similar concept in stan.
>
> The key in bugs/jags is that you're always in one model or another.
> When in model 1, you're estimating model 1 with some probability of switching to model 2, where model 2's "priors" are evaluated as the posterior of model 2 (previously estimated). The latter is *only* to make jumping easier. I don't think it's actually required for computing the BF in theory, it just helps with mixing.
>
> Could one do something analogous?
> In stan, one can pit two models against each other as a mixture; (p[1]likelihood[1] + p[2]likelihood[2])*priors.
> I tried this and of course it didn't seem to 'work'; I had an intercept-only model and a full model, and the probability of each was roughly .5 (no change from prior of ~logistic(0,1)).
> Or several chains would converge to suggest p[1] was much higher, although BayesFactor suggests the opposite (this seems highly dependent on initial values).
> I'm using the example from the BayesFactor package (below).
>
> Is it possible to conditionally set priors, or to 'weight' the priors themselves by the probability of each model?
>
>
> library(BayesFactor)
> library(rstan)
> data(attitude)
> ds <- attitude
> ds <- scale(ds)
> options(mc.cores=parallel::detectCores())
> rstan_options(auto_write=TRUE)
>
> bf.stan <- "
> data{
> int N;
> int J;
> matrix[N,J] y;
> }
>
> parameters {
> vector[6] beta;
> real intercept[2];
> real<lower=0> resid[2];
> real p_logis;
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
> simplex[2] p;
>
> p[2] <- exp(p_logis)/(1 + exp(p_logis));
> p[1] <- 1 - p[2];
> }
>
> model {
> real lp_k[2];
> real lp;
> vector[N] yhat[2];
> beta ~ cauchy(0,1);
> intercept ~ cauchy(0,1);
> resid ~ cauchy(0,1);
> p_logis ~ logistic(0,1);
>
> for(n in 1:N){
> yhat[1,n] <- intercept[1];
> yhat[2,n] <- intercept[2] + y[n,2:7]*beta;
> }
> lp_k[1] <- log(p[1]) + normal_log(y'[1],yhat[1],rep_vector(resid[1],N));
> lp_k[2] <- log(p[2]) + normal_log(y'[1],yhat[2],rep_vector(resid[2],N));
> lp <- log_sum_exp(lp_k);
> increment_log_prob(lp);
> }
> "
> stanOut <- stan(model_code=bf.stan,data=list(y=ds,N=30,J=7),iter=10000,chains=8)

>
>
>
>
